summary: Mysterium is a cooperative deduction party game where one player acts as a mute ghost communicating clues through surreal illustrated cards while the rest of the table tries to guess a suspect, location, and weapon. It's a beloved, atmospheric icebreaker that thrives on wild interpretation and shared laughter rather than tight logic.
praised: unique asymmetric ghost role is memorable
criticised: luck-dependent on which clue cards you're dealt
ghost player can feel passive/frustrated if clues don't align
less satisfying with very analytical groups expecting tight logic

interaction.kind: cooperative clue-giving and group discussion to interpret shared vision cards
interaction.detail: The ghost communicates through cards visible to specific mediums, who then discuss and vote as a group to converge on the solution, so nearly all game state (the clues, the guesses, the shrinking suspect pool) is shared. There's no personal board at all; the whole game is players affecting each other's interpretation of the same evidence.
interaction.said: unknown, but as a cooperative party deduction game it's built entirely around mediums discussing and interpreting the same visions together

scoring.how_you_win: There's no score; the mediums win by correctly deducing the culprit, location, and weapon from the ghost's visions, then confirming it with a correct final guess, all before the clock of vision cards runs out.

similar: Detective: A Modern Crime Board Game

theme.said: often called a reskinned Dixit/Clue hybrid, 'the ghost theme is flavor over a picture-clue guessing game', though some say the vision-card interpretation genuinely feels séance-like
theme.why: a ghost silently handing over surreal dream-image cards that mediums must interpret models the séance premise reasonably well, but the underlying deduction structure (match clue-cards to suspect/location/weapon) is the same abstract logic engine as any Clue-style game

style.why: It is fully cooperative with no conflict or elimination, but the real-time guessing and storytelling make the experience matter far more than any optimization.
